messages.subject_clean: tz issues with scale_x_datetime with ggplot2 2.0.0?
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am having issues with setting tz properly with the new ggplot2, v2.0.0.

My input data is set to PST, however, the graph outputs in UTC.

  ggplot(data=d, aes(x=TIMEOFDAY, y=USAGE)) +
    geom_line(aes(group=DATE))  +
     xlab("Time of Day") +
     ylab("Demand (kW)")  +
     scale_x_datetime(date_labels="%H:%M %Z", date_breaks="2 hours")

In older versions of ggplot2, I did not specifically set tz in the plot function.  As long as the input data had tz set, my plot used the intended timezone.

The scale_x_datetime function does not seem to accept a "tz" argument.

Any ideas how to control tz in the display?

Thanks!
Emily

messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

Try replacing

date_labels = "..."

with

labels = date_format("...", tz = "...").

This assumes you are using the scales package. So the result should be:
ggplot(data=d, aes(x=TIMEOFDAY, y=USAGE)) +
    geom_line(aes(group=DATE))  +
    xlab("Time of Day") +
    ylab("Demand (kW)")  +
    scale_x_datetime(
        labels = date_format("%H:%M %Z",
                             tz = "PST"),
        date_breaks="2 hours"
    )

Does this work for you?

Sherif

it (it would require the agreement of all copyright holders who are

messages.body_plain:
Your example is not reproducible, so let's try one:

set.seed(2530)
DF <- data.frame(A = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 1000, replace = TRUE),
                 B = sample(letters[1:2], 1000, replace = TRUE))

library(dplyr)
DFsumm <- DF %>% group_by(A, B) %>% summarise(freq = n())

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DFsumm, aes(x = A, y = freq, fill = B)) +
   geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
   geom_text(aes(y = freq + 3, label = freq),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.9))

Does that do what you want?

BTW, a useful reference for standard ggplot2 graphics, apart from the
on-line help pages, is Winston Chang's excellent "R Graphics
Cookbook", published by O'Reilly, which contains several variations on
this type of example. You can also look to the companion site
http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/, although this particular example is
not covered there.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
If you use a grey scale for the points you want to deemphasize, there
should be no problem:

mycolours1 <- c("U" = "darkgreen", "D" = "red", "N"="grey50")
mycolours2 <- c("U" = "darkgreen", "D" = "red", "N"="grey90")
mycolours3 <- c("U" = "darkgreen", "D" = "red", "N"="blue")

library(ggplot2)

# Notice that the levels of z are set in the data frame
# (Aside: Why did I define it this way instead of copying yours?)
DF <- data.frame(x = seq(6), y = seq(6),
                 z = factor(rep(c("U", "D", "N"), each = 2),
                            levels = c("U", "D", "N")))

# Modify grey scale
ggplot(data = DF, aes(y = y, x = x)) +
                 theme_bw() +
                 geom_point(size=3, aes(colour=z)) +
                 scale_colour_manual("Status", values = mycolours1)

# Higher values of grey produce lighter shades
ggplot(data = DF, aes(y = y, x = x)) +
                 theme_bw() +
                 geom_point(size=3, aes(colour=z)) +
                 scale_colour_manual("Status", values = mycolours2)

Just tweak the grey value to produce the effect you want.

Another approach is to map the alpha transparency level (aka
'opacity') of each mapped color value. In your example, the levels of
z are "D", "N" and "U", so you can define the values of the opacity
vector accordingly. (This was why I set the levels in the data frame,
BTW.)

# Modify opacity (alpha)
ggplot(data = DF, aes(y = y, x = x)) +
                 theme_bw() +
                 geom_point(size=3, aes(colour=z)) +
                 scale_colour_manual("Status", values = mycolours3)

opacity <- c(1, 1, 0.2)    # values correspond to the level ordering of z
ggplot(data = DF, aes(y = y, x = x)) +
                 theme_bw() +
                 geom_point(size=3, aes(colour=z)) +
                 scale_colour_manual("Status",
                      values = alpha(mycolours3, opacity))

Again, you can adjust the values of opacity to taste.

Dennis

Hi,

 I just encountered a strange behaviour when using a stacked geom_bar with scale_y_sqrt.
Stacked bars (with more than one stack element) which are the same total height in normal scale have differing total heights in transformed sqrt scale.

To me it looks like a bug. At least its not the behaviour I would expect.

Any ideas?

Best,
Daniel

Example:

ggplot(d, aes(x=x, fill=fill)) + geom_bar(aes(y=y), stat="identity", position="stack")

ggplot(d, aes(x=x, fill=fill)) + geom_bar(aes(y=y), stat="identity", position="stack") + scale_y_sqrt()

# With ggvis, the result is as expected:
ggvis(d, x=~x, y=~y, fill=~fill) %>% layer_bars() %>% scale_numeric("y", trans="sqrt")

messages.subject: Re: Transformed y scale breaks stacked bar chart
messages.subject_clean: Transformed y scale breaks stacked bar chart
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 applies transformations at various points in the process of
training a ggplot, in the following order:

scale transformations (effected by scale_ functions);
statistical transformations (effected by stat_ functions);
coordinate transformations (effected by coord_ functions).

geom_bar() calls stat_bin(), so the bar plots occur after statistical
transformation. Thus, when you use scale_y_sqrt(), it transforms the
y's before passing it to stat_bin(), which is why you don't get what
you expected.

OTOH, coordinate scaling takes place after statistical transformation,
so a coordinate change affects both the y-scale and the bars. So the
following code does what you expected:

d <- data.frame(x=factor(c(1,1,2)), y=c(1,2,3), fill=factor(c(1,2,3)))

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, fill = fill)) +
   geom_bar(aes(y = y), stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
   coord_trans(y = "sqrt")

This ordering is documented in both the first and second editions of
Hadley's ggplot2 book, the latter of which is forthcoming. To answer
your question, the behavior is not a bug - it's a design feature of
which you were apparently unaware.

Notice that the ggvis() call uses trans =  inside scale_numeric(); it
borrows from ggplot2::coord_trans().

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Uh, no. The OP has 5 values in 1986 and 4 in 2005. For a boxplot, one
should have at least 20 observations per group, preferably 30 or more.
In this case, I'd suggest a strip chart, which is simply a
geom_point() layer, perhaps one of the following:

library(ggplot2)

DF <- data.frame(X1, X2)

# Treats X2 as numeric
ggplot(DF, aes(x = X2, y = X1)) + geom_point()

# Treats X2 as factor
ggplot(DF, aes(x = factor(X2), y = X1)) + geom_point() +
   labs(x = "X2")

Another problem with boxplots or error bars in this context is that
they don't reflect the large difference in sample size in 2004
relative to 1986 or 2005 unless you add sample size annotations
somewhere in the graphics region.

Alternatives if one only wants to visualize point ranges include
geom_pointrange() and geom_linerange(). See the on-line help for
additional details: docs.ggplot2.org/current <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current>

Dennis

The charts are too big? You should set this when opening the device you
want to save them to. For example, use ggplot to create a ggplot object

my.plot <- ggplot(DF)+geom_line(aes(x=d,y=v))
pdf("myplot.pdf",height=3,width=7) # to save to pdf 3 inches high, 7 wide
print(my.plot) # print your ggplot object to the device
dev.off() # close the device

You might find you then need to have a couple of attempts tweaking font
sizes etc in your ggplot object with theme(). See ?theme

Regards,
Ron.

messages.subject: Forcing full legends even with missing data values
messages.subject_clean: Forcing full legends even with missing data values
messages.body_plain:
I am using ggplot to generate maps with telemetry data over time, which I then compile together into animations.  The data is spotty, that is to say maps from some time steps have no data, and others have only a single point.  Because I'm animating these over a whole season, what I'd like is to force the full legend onto all plots so that it doesn't change (e.g. flicker on and off) during the animation.

The legends I'm using now are scale_size_manual for point size (factor with 3 possible values) and a color gradient for point color, just using the defaults so there's no scale command.  The relevant commands for a single plot include:
geom_point(data=these.tagpoints, aes(x=long, y=lat, color=maxsig, size=qty.bin))+
scale_size_manual("Tag Hits",values=c(2,3,4), labels=ptsizelabels,drop=FALSE)

Giving you code to reproduce is problematic as it plots on base map data separately created but necessary for the plot.  I could take time to hack it down to something smaller if it's necessary.  I thought I'd try asking first to see if anyone has tried this.  The "drop=FALSE" command does not do the trick for me (am I using it correctly?)  Regardless, the full range of values for the gradient aren't going to be in the current plot anyway.

In the past I have played around with having dummy data with the full range of values but plotted hidden or invisible.  Perhaps that's what I'd need to do for this.  The only way I know to make points invisible is to set their size to zero, which obviously won't work for me as I need a range of sizes; setting color to transparent won't work for the same reason.

Another thought I had was to make one plot that has all the values and somehow just save the legends as an object which I could add on later, perhaps using grid.arrange.  I'd love some tips on how to do that.

library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)
library(scales)

df.2 <- df.1 %>%
  select(Season,Division, Level,X)

df.2$Delta = as.numeric(gsub("%","",df.2$X))

df.3 <- df.2 %>%
  filter(Level != "Avg") %>%
  arrange(Delta)

df.4 = df.3 %>%
  select(Season,Level,Delta)

p3 = ggplot(df.4, aes (x = Level,y = Delta, fill = Season)) +
  geom_bar(
    stat = "identity",
    position = position_dodge(),
    size = .3

  theme_bw() +
